claims.claim: On 21 June 2026 the Sun rises at about 4:05 a.m. IST at Dong, Arunachal Pradesh (97.0°E), and about 6:08 a.m. IST in western Kutch, Gujarat (68.8°E): just over two hours apart, although both keep the same clock.

claims.notes: Sunrise in Dong is often reported as 'around 4 a.m.' in summer; the computed 4:05 agrees. Pin coordinates (Dong 97.02E 28.17N; western Kutch 68.8E 23.8N) and the clock range shown (3:50 to 6:15 IST, offset 5.5 h) are the inputs of the calculation. City clocks: Ahmedabad 72.58E 23.03N, Delhi 77.21E 28.61N, Kolkata 88.36E 22.57N, Guwahati 91.74E 26.14N. Computed sunrise on 21 June 2026 (IST): Guwahati 4:31, Kolkata 4:52, Delhi 5:23, Ahmedabad 5:54.

claims.claim: After independence in 1947 India adopted one standard time, IST (UTC+5:30, set by the 82.5°E meridian), for the whole country. Bombay kept its own local time until 1955.

sources.title: CSIR-National Physical Laboratory: Indian Standard Time

contradictions: Calcutta kept its own time until 1948 by some accounts.

claims.claim: In 2018 researchers at CSIR-National Physical Laboratory, India's timekeeper, proposed in Current Science two time zones: IST-I (UTC+5:30) and IST-II (UTC+6:30) for the north-east, divided at 89°52′E. India still keeps one.

sources.title: Current Science (2018): two time zones for India, CSIR-NPL researchers
Reporting on the NPL proposal (The Hindu, 2018)
